2027-07-27.title: Tuesday of the Seventeenth Week in Ordinary Time
readings: The Lord used to speak to Moses face to face, as one speaks to a friend
The Lord is kind and merciful
Explain to us the parable of the weeds of the field
2027-07-27.alt: Weekday of Ordinary Time, Week 17 (Year I). The first reading continues the story of Moses and the covenant at Sinai, read on the weekdays of weeks 15 to 17. In Kerala this is the season when farmers weed and tend the young paddy in the rain. Liturgical colour: green.
2027-07-27.verse: The Lord passed before him, and proclaimed, “The Lord, the Lord, a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness
theo: After the golden calf the Lord said he would not go in the midst of this people (Exodus 33:3), and so Moses does something quiet and brave: he takes the tent, pitches it “outside the camp, far off from the camp,” and calls it the tent of meeting. “Everyone who sought the Lord would go out to the tent.” It is a place open to anyone who wants to pray. When Moses enters, the pillar of cloud comes down at the entrance, and the whole people, each at the door of their own tent, rise and bow down. Then comes the sentence that is at the heart of today's reading: “Thus the Lord used to speak to Moses face to face, as one speaks to a friend.” Moses returns to the camp, but young Joshua “would not leave the tent.” Some people cannot bear to leave the place where God speaks. In chapter 34 Moses goes up the mountain a second time, and the Lord comes down in the cloud and “proclaimed the name”: “The Lord, the Lord, a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness, keeping steadfast love for the thousandth generation, forgiving iniquity and transgression and sin.” This is the great self-portrait of God in the Old Testament, repeated by the Psalms, the prophets and Jonah. It holds mercy and justice together (“yet by no means clearing the guilty”), but notice the proportions: judgment reaches “the third and the fourth generation,” while steadfast love reaches “the thousandth.” Moses bows quickly and prays, and his prayer is bold: “Although this is a stiff-necked people, pardon our iniquity and our sin, and take us for your inheritance.” He uses their stubbornness as his argument for God to come with them. Then he spends “forty days and forty nights” with the Lord, neither eating nor drinking, and writes the words of the covenant. The Psalm sings it back: “The Lord is merciful and gracious, slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love. As far as the east is from the west, so far he removes our transgressions from us.”

In the Gospel, away from the crowds and “in the house,” the disciples ask Jesus: “Explain to us the parable of the weeds of the field.” He gives them a key: the one who sows is the Son of Man; the field is the world; the good seed are “the children of the kingdom”; the weeds are “the children of the evil one”; the enemy is the devil; the harvest is the end of the age and the reapers are angels. We should read the explanation together with the parable itself. When the servants asked whether they should pull up the weeds, the householder said: “No; for in gathering the weeds you would uproot the wheat along with them. Let both of them grow together until the harvest.” That is God's patience, the “slow to anger” of Exodus 34. We are not the reapers. We are told to sow, to weed our own hearts and to leave the final sorting to the Lord, because we cannot always tell wheat from weeds, and a person who looks like a weed today may be wheat tomorrow. The saints began as sinners. But the parable is serious too. There will be a harvest; “all causes of sin and all evildoers” will be gathered, and the end is described in terrible words. The Church teaches that Christ will come to judge the living and the dead (Catechism 678–679) and she does not soften the warning; yet she does not name anyone as lost. And the parable ends in light: “Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father,” echoing the prophet Daniel: “those who lead many to righteousness, like the stars forever and ever.” The Church herself is a field where wheat and weeds grow, “holy and always in need of purification” (Catechism 827), and the patience of God is what gives each of us time to turn. St Peter says it plainly: the Lord “is patient with you, not wanting any to perish, but all to come to repentance” (2 Peter 3:9).
outline: Ask: with whom can you talk as you talk to a friend, and is God one of them?
The tent outside the camp: God speaks to Moses as to a friend, and Joshua will not leave.
Point 2 · The name of the Lord
Merciful and gracious, slow to anger: mercy reaches to the thousandth generation.
The patience of God gives time; we sow and weed our own hearts, and the harvest is the Lord's.
“The Lord, the Lord, a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness.”
live: Spend ten minutes before the tabernacle or in silent prayer today, and speak to God plainly, as to a friend: tell him what is on your mind.
Before you judge someone this week, pray for them, and name one good seed in them. Weed your own heart first, with the help of confession.
2027-07-27.prayer: Merciful and gracious God, slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love, you spoke to Moses face to face as to a friend, and in your Son you call us your friends. Give us the courage to pitch our tent of prayer outside the noise of the camp, and to stay near it like Joshua. Teach us your patience, that we may not pull up the wheat while we judge the weeds, but leave the harvest to you. Make us shine like the sun in the kingdom of our Father. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.
altar: In every church the tabernacle is the tent of meeting. The little red lamp tells us that he is there, the Lord who spoke to Moses as to a friend and who now says to us in the Gospel: “I have called you friends” (John 15:15). At Mass, in the Kyrie, we cry out to the Lord for mercy, and just before Communion we pray: Lamb of God, you take away the sins of the world, have mercy on us. The name proclaimed to Moses, “merciful and gracious,” is placed in our hands in the Eucharist; and the same Lord who is patient with weeds feeds us with his own Body and Blood so that we may become wheat.

quick: Moses pitches a tent of meeting outside the camp, where the Lord speaks to him face to face, as to a friend; Joshua will not leave the tent.
The Lord proclaims his name to Moses: merciful and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness.
Jesus explains the parable of the weeds: the Son of Man sows, the harvest is the end of the age, and the righteous will shine like the sun.
2027-07-27.action: Spend ten quiet minutes today talking to God as to a friend.
2027-07-27.question: Am I patient with the weeds I see in others and in myself, or do I want to pull everything up now?
kidsaint: Moses had a special tent where he went to talk to God. The people stood at the doors of their own tents and watched, and when the big cloud came down they all bowed. The Bible says that God spoke to Moses face to face, as one speaks to a friend. Moses was not perfect, but he kept coming back to talk to God and he asked God to forgive his people. Lesson: God wants to be our friend, and we can talk to him anywhere, any time.

family.explain: Moses had a tent where he went to talk to God, and God spoke to him like a friend. We can talk to God like that too, in church or in our room. In the Gospel Jesus tells a story about a farmer who sowed good seed, but an enemy sowed weeds in the field. The farmer said: do not pull up the weeds now, or you will pull up the wheat. Let both grow until the harvest. God is patient with us, even when we do wrong, and he gives us time to grow.
family.intention: We pray for those who find it hard to forgive and for people we find difficult.
family.ask: Ask: “Where can we each find a quiet place to talk to God? Who needs our patience this week?”

illus: A farmer in Kuttanad who tended his paddy through the monsoon told a young neighbour that the hardest part was not planting but weeding. When the young man pulled up weeds in a hurry, he often pulled out the rice with them. The old farmer said: you wait until the weed shows itself, and you pull only what you are sure of. Years later the young man, now a school headmaster, used the same lesson with a boy who was always in trouble. He waited, and he watched, and one day the boy brought him a prize from a science fair. The headmaster said it was the wheat that had been growing all along. (An illustrative story.)

pm.open: Merciful and gracious God, you speak to us as friends and you are slow to anger. Teach us to listen, to be patient and to trust your harvest. Amen.
share: The Lord used to speak to Moses face to face, as one speaks to a friend (Exodus 33:11). When did I last speak to God as to a friend?
The Lord, the Lord, a God merciful and gracious (Exodus 34:6). Which word in this name of God do I most need to hear today?
Let both of them grow together until the harvest (Matthew 13:30). Whom do I need to be more patient with?
pm.resp: The Lord is kind and merciful.
interc: For the Church, a field of wheat and weeds, that she may be a place of patience, mercy and conversion.
For priests and confessors, that they may show the mercy of the God who is slow to anger.
For farmers and labourers who tend the young crops in the rain, and for a good harvest.
For those who judge others harshly, and for those who have been judged unfairly, that all may find God's mercy.
For our group, that we may pray as friends of God and be patient with each other.
pm.close: Father, you are merciful and gracious, slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love. Keep us patient until the harvest and bring us to shine in your kingdom. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

homily: Dear friends, after the sin of the golden calf, Moses does a beautiful thing. He pitches a tent outside the camp, far from the noise, and calls it the tent of meeting. And anyone who wants to seek the Lord can go there. When Moses goes in, the cloud comes down, and the people stand at the doors of their tents and bow. And the Bible says: the Lord used to speak to Moses face to face, as one speaks to a friend (Exodus 33:11).

Do we speak to God like that? We say many prayers, but do we ever just talk? Moses returns to the camp, but Joshua, the young man, would not leave the tent. Some people cannot leave the place where God speaks. Do we have a quiet place, a corner of the house, a church, a chapel, where we can sit with the Lord, who now waits for us in the tabernacle?

And what does God say about himself when he passes before Moses? The Lord, the Lord, a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness (Exodus 34:6). Notice: slow to anger. Moses bows to the ground, and he prays: although this is a stiff-necked people, pardon our iniquity and our sin. He knows he is asking for a lot, but he knows to whom he is asking.

The Gospel shows the same patience. The farmer sowed good seed, and an enemy sowed weeds. The servants want to tear them out at once. But the master says: no, you would uproot the wheat along with them. Let both grow until the harvest. Brothers and sisters, God is waiting for the weeds in us to turn. We are not the judges. We are the ones who have been given time. Let us use it: weed our own hearts, confess our sins, forgive those who wrong us, and be patient with others. And at the harvest, the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father. Amen.
kids: Children, Moses had a special tent where he went to talk to God. God spoke to him like a friend. We can talk to God like a friend too, at home, in church and on the way to school. And Jesus told a story about a farmer who found weeds growing among the wheat. He did not pull them up at once, because he might hurt the good plants. God is patient with us too. Let us thank him today, and let us be patient with our brothers and sisters!

intro: Theme: “The Lord, the Lord, a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger.”
The tent of meeting, the name of the Lord, and the patient farmer: God speaks as to a friend and waits for the harvest.

points.h: Face to face, as to a friend
q: Thus the Lord used to speak to Moses face to face, as one speaks to a friend.

I do not call you servants any longer, because the servant does not know what the master is doing; but I have called you friends, because I have made known to you everything that I have heard from my Father.
points.apply: Choose a fixed time and place for a quiet talk with God each day this week, and keep it.

q: The Lord is merciful and gracious, slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love.
The Lord is not slow about his promise, as some think of slowness, but is patient with you, not wanting any to perish, but all to come to repentance.
points.apply: Go to confession this week and let the God who is slow to anger forgive you, then forgive one person who has wronged you.

sub: Let both grow until the harvest.
The righteous will shine like the sun.
q: Those who are wise shall shine like the brightness of the sky, and those who lead many to righteousness, like the stars forever and ever.
Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father. Let anyone with ears listen!
points.apply: Be patient this week with one person you have been quick to judge, and look for the good seed in them.

concl: God speaks to Moses as to a friend and proclaims his name: merciful and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in steadfast love.
Jesus explains that the field is the world and that the harvest belongs to the Lord, so that we may use our time to sow good seed and turn to him.
2027-07-27.resolve: Spend ten minutes a day this week talking to God as to a friend, and be patient with one difficult person.
